section.title: Additional topics: local existence and uniqueness

introduction.p: used initial conditions to select solutions, but this selection requires hypotheses on the slope law. We can now give a precise theorem and prove it using completeness, uniform convergence, and the contraction theorem. This optional section can be read independently of the complex-number and Fourier material in this chapter.

subsection.title: A Lipschitz condition in the dependent variable
subsection.p: Consider y'=F(t,y), y(t_0)=y_0. Fix positive a,b and the rectangle
The law is Lipschitz in y on R if one constant L\ge0 satisfies

whenever (t,u),(t,v)\in R. The same L must work for every time in the rectangle. A bound |\partial F/\partial y|\le L suffices: this derivative means differentiating with respect to y while holding t fixed, and the one-variable Mean Value Theorem applies. Lipschitz continuity does not require that derivative to exist; F(t,y)=|y| is Lipschitz with L=1.

theorem.title: A local existence and uniqueness theorem

statement.p: Suppose F is continuous on R, satisfies the Lipschitz condition above, and |F(t,y)|\le M on R. Choose h>0 so that

Then there is a continuously differentiable solution on I=[t_0-h,t_0+h] with y(t_0)=y_0 and |y(t)-y_0|\le b. It is unique among solutions on I whose graphs stay in R. In particular, the initial value problem has a unique local solution near t_0.

subsection.p: The stated bounds M and L determine a positive interval length. There is always a positive admissible h; for example, h=\min\{a,b/(M+1),1/(2(L+1))\} works, including when M=0 or L=0. The theorem provides a guaranteed local interval, which need not be the largest possible interval.

subsection.title: Proof by successive approximations
subsection.p: Integrating the differential equation gives the equivalent integral equation
Let D consist of continuous functions u:I\to\mathbb R satisfying |u(t)-y_0|\le b. Measure distance by the uniform distance

This is a metric, and D is complete. Indeed, a Cauchy sequence in this metric is Cauchy at each point, hence has a pointwise real limit by . Taking the limit in the uniform Cauchy bound shows uniform convergence to that function. The uniform-limit theorem preserves continuity, and taking pointwise limits preserves |u(t)-y_0|\le b. Thus the limit belongs to D.

The contraction constant is q=Lh<1. By , T has a unique fixed point y in D. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus shows that this fixed point is continuously differentiable and solves the differential equation. Conversely, every solution with graph in R satisfies the integral equation, so uniqueness of the fixed point proves the stated uniqueness. Any other local solution is close to y_0 by continuity and hence stays in R on a sufficiently small interval; the same contraction argument on that interval shows that the two local solutions agree there.

example.title: Picard iterates for exponential growth
example.p: For y'=y, y(0)=1, take a=1, b=1, M=2, L=1, and h=1/2. The iterates are u_0=1, u_1=1+t, u_2=1+t+t^2/2, and in general u_n=\sum_{k=0}^n t^k/k!. Their uniform limit is e^t. Picard iteration integrates an entire previous function; Euler and Runge–Kutta methods instead advance numerical values along a grid.

subsection.title: What the hypotheses do and do not guarantee

example.title: Continuity alone does not guarantee uniqueness
example.p: The law F(t,y)=2\sqrt{|y|} is continuous but not Lipschitz near y=0, since |F(t,u)-F(t,0)|/|u|=2/\sqrt u for u>0. For the initial data y(0)=0, the zero solution and every function
solve the equation. At t=c, both one-sided derivatives are zero, so these are actual differentiable solutions. The solution may wait and then depart. Initial data alone do not force uniqueness.

figure.caption: Three solutions of y'=2\sqrt{|y|} pass through (0,0): immediate departure, departure after time one, and the zero solution.

description.p: On the interval from minus one to two, a parabola beginning at time zero, a parabola beginning at time one, and the zero solution all coincide initially on the horizontal axis.

example.title: Without continuity, existence can fail
example.p: Define F(y)=1 if y=0 and F(y)=0 otherwise. There is no differentiable solution of y'=F(y) with y(0)=0 on a neighborhood of zero. A solution would have y'(0)=1, hence y(t)>0 for all sufficiently small positive t. There its derivative would be zero, forcing it to be constant by the Mean Value Theorem. Continuity at zero would make that constant zero, a contradiction.

subsection.p: Lipschitz continuity is sufficient for uniqueness, but not necessary. For y'=-\sqrt[3]{y}, y(0)=0, the law is not Lipschitz at zero, yet the zero solution is the only forward solution. Along any differentiable solution, (y^2)'=-2|y|^{4/3}\le0. Starting from y^2=0, nonnegativity forces y=0 for future times. This statement concerns forward uniqueness; backward departure is possible.

warning.title: Local does not mean global
warning.p: The smooth law y'=y^2, y(0)=1, has the unique solution y=1/(1-t) near zero, but the solution becomes unbounded at time one. Local existence and uniqueness do not imply that a solution continues for all time.

statement.p: Apply the theorem to y'=t+y^2, y(0)=1, on |t|\le1, |y-1|\le1. Find valid M,L,h. Then verify the waiting solutions in the nonuniqueness example at the joining point.
